title: Ebola, Twitter, and misinformation: A dangerous combination?
screen_reason: Two-page BMJ letter reporting a content analysis of all English-language tweets containing 'Ebola' and 'prevention' or 'cure' posted from Guinea, Liberia and Nigeria during 1-7 September 2014. Table 1 gives the share of tweets classified as medical misinformation (313, 55.5%) against medically correct (203, 36%) and other (48, 8.5%), and the text gives the share of retweeted tweets carrying misinformation (146/248, 58.9%). Both are quantitative shares with denominators.

estimates.measure_type: % of English-language Ebola prevention/cure tweets from Guinea, Liberia and Nigeria classified as medical misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 313 (55.5%) medical misinformation; 203 (36%) medically correct information; 48 (8.5%) other, including tweets of a spiritual nature
estimates.denominator: all English-language tweets containing the terms 'Ebola' and 'prevention' or 'cure' posted from Guinea, Liberia and Nigeria during 1-7 September 2014 (203 + 313 + 48 = 564 tweets; the letter never states the total)
estimates.definition: A tweet counted in the numerator if the authors grouped it as medical misinformation rather than medically correct information or other. The commonest examples given are that Ebola might be cured by the plant ewedu or by unqualified blood transfusion, and that drinking and washing in salty water help.
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition. The operational statement is: "We grouped them into medically correct information, medical misinformation, and other (including tweets of a spiritual nature)."
estimates.n: 564 tweets (derived from the three category counts; not stated in the letter)
estimates.page_loc: Table 1, p. 2, row 'Tweets (%)', under the column headings 'Medically correct information / Medical misinformation / Other (including tweets of a spiritual nature)'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: The authors (a clinician in Nigeria, a research psychologist and a professor in Norway) grouped the tweets into the three categories. Being a letter, the piece states no coding protocol, no number of coders, no adjudication procedure and no reliability statistic; the chi-square test reported (P<0.001) concerns the distribution across categories, not agreement.
estimates.moderator_quote: We used the Twitter search engine to collect all tweets in English with the terms "Ebola" and "prevention" or "cure" from Guinea, Liberia, and Nigeria during 1 to 7 September 2014.
estimates.notes: The 55.5% is verbatim in Table 1; the denominator of 564 is the sum of the three verbatim category counts and is corroborated by the text's '248 (44%) were retweeted at least once' (248/564 = 44.0%). Confidence is medium not because the number is unclear but because this is a two-page letter with no stated coding procedure and no reliability, and a one-week keyword window in three countries. Also note the collection is restricted to English-language tweets, which in Guinea and Liberia is a serious language filter.

estimates.measure_type: % of the Ebola tweets that were retweeted at least once which contained medical misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 146 of 248 retweeted tweets (58.9%); 95 contained scientifically correct information (38.3%); 7 other
estimates.denominator: 248 of the collected tweets (44%) that were retweeted at least once
estimates.definition: Among tweets retweeted at least once, the share the authors grouped as medical misinformation rather than scientifically correct information or other.
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition. The operational statement is: "We grouped them into medically correct information, medical misinformation, and other (including tweets of a spiritual nature)."
estimates.page_loc: Letter text, p. 1 (sentence beginning 'Among these tweets, 248 (44%) were retweeted at least once'); Table 1 'Retweets*' row (95 / 146 / 7)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same categorisation by the authors as for the full corpus; no coding protocol or reliability statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: Most tweets and retweets contained misinformation, and misinformation had a much larger potential reach than correct information (table).
estimates.notes: The full sentence is 'Among these tweets, 248 (44%) were retweeted at least once; 95 of these contained scientifically correct information (38.3%), whereas 146 contained medical misinformation (58.9%; P<0.001).'; the two-column text file interleaves it with the reference list, so the quoted span is the contiguous clause carrying the value. Coded SHARING with sharing_subtype content_share: the denominator is the set of items that were actually reshared, so the value answers 'of what got retweeted, how much was misinformation'. One reading risk: the sentence opens 'Among these tweets', which follows a sentence about misinformation examples, but 248/564 = 44% and 95 of the 248 being medically correct both show the base is the whole corpus, not the misinformation subset. This row is nested inside the CONTENT row's corpus and is not independent of it. The paper does not report how many retweets each tweet received, so a retweet-weighted share is not available.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) The exposure-weighted share was NOT extracted although it is the most reviewer-relevant number in the letter. Table 1 gives potential readers of 15,039,097 for misinformation, 5,596,153 for correct information and 48,308 for other; misinformation would be 15,039,097 / 20,683,558 = 72.7% of potential readership. The letter states only that 'misinformation had a much larger potential reach than correct information' and never gives a percentage or a total, so the value would rest on a cross-category sum I computed, which R8 forbids. Recorded here in full so an adjudicator can rule; if allowed it would be an EXPOSURE row (exposure_type proportion, denom_scope topical) and a much higher figure than the 55.5% item share. Note also that 'potential readers' is a follower-count reach proxy, not observed impressions. (2) Two individual tweets are named with their retweet counts (23 and 24); single-item counts are not estimates. (3) No respondent-level, panel or concentration data exist in this letter. (4) The letter gives no total tweet count, no sampling detail beyond the query, and no coder or reliability information, all of which limit every row.

rob.design: One-week keyword census on Twitter reported as a BMJ letter. Frame: all English-language tweets containing 'Ebola' and 'prevention' or 'cure' posted from Guinea, Liberia and Nigeria, 1-7 September 2014, retrieved through the Twitter search engine; 564 tweets by summation, of which 248 were retweeted at least once. Classification into medically correct information, medical misinformation and other was done by the authors, with no stated codebook, no number of coders, no adjudication rule and no inter-rater reliability; a chi-square test across categories is reported at P<0.001. Reach is measured as 'potential readers', a follower-based upper bound rather than observed exposure. The English-language restriction and the seven-day window are the main frame limitations, and the letter format means the methods cannot be audited further.
rob.item6_quote: We grouped them into medically correct information, medical misinformation, and other (including tweets of a spiritual nature).
rob.item10_quote: Among these tweets, 248 (44%) were retweeted at least once; 95 of these contained scientifically correct information (38.3%), whereas 146 contained medical misinformation (58.9%; P<0.001).
